transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new program launched by the Royal Mail in the United Kingdom is aiming to turn postmen and women into community health first responders. The initiative, which began as a pilot in rural areas last year, is now being rolled out across 500 towns and villages. Postal workers, who already visit every household daily as part of their regular rounds, are being trained to recognize signs of common health emergencies such as strokes, heart attacks, and severe allergic reactions. They carry basic first aid kits and are equipped with portable defibrillators in their delivery vans. According to Royal Mail officials, postal workers are often the only regular visitors to elderly residents living alone in remote communities, making them ideally positioned to notice when something might be wrong. In the first six months of the pilot program, postal workers helped save 17 lives by responding quickly to emergencies they encountered during their rounds. The program has received praise from health charities, which say it could significantly improve emergency response times in underserved areas.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: Scientists at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute have made a remarkable discovery deep in the Pacific Ocean: a new species of giant phantom jellyfish that was previously unknown to science. The creature was spotted at a depth of approximately 1,200 meters during a remotely operated vehicle dive off the coast of California. What makes this jellyfish particularly unusual is its size—its bell measures over one meter across, and its four ribbon-like oral arms extend more than 10 meters in length. Unlike most jellyfish that pulse their bells to move, this giant species appears to drift passively with ocean currents, using its long arms to trap small fish and plankton. Marine biologists say the discovery highlights how little we still know about life in the deep ocean, which remains one of the most unexplored environments on Earth. The research team has collected several specimens for further study and is working to formally describe and name the new species. They note that similar jellyfish have been captured on camera only about a dozen times in the past 30 years, making this an extremely rare find.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A growing number of companies across Japan are introducing "workation" programs that allow employees to work remotely from vacation destinations. The concept, which combines work and vacation, has gained popularity as companies seek ways to prevent employee burnout while maintaining productivity. Under these programs, staff can spend weeks or even months working from beach resorts, mountain lodges, or other scenic locations, provided they complete their assigned tasks and attend required meetings. Several major Japanese corporations have reported that employees who participate in workation programs show increased creativity and job satisfaction. The Japanese government has also been promoting the initiative as a way to stimulate tourism in regional areas that have suffered from population decline. Local businesses in popular workation destinations report a significant increase in long-term stays, with many hotels and guesthouses renovating rooms to include dedicated workspaces and high-speed internet. However, critics argue that the boundary between work and leisure becomes blurred, potentially leading to employees working longer hours than they would in the office.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (David): Sarah, I'm thinking about joining a gym, but there are so many around here. Do you belong to one? You seem pretty fit.
Woman (Sarah): Thanks, David! Actually, I don't go to a traditional gym. I go to that new boxing studio on the high street—you know, the one that opened last spring?
Man: Boxing? That sounds intense! I've never done anything like that before. I was thinking something more low-key, maybe with cardio machines and weights.

Woman: Oh, don't let the word "boxing" scare you! They have classes for all fitness levels, and most people who go are just regular people looking to get in shape, not serious fighters. It's actually really fun—way more engaging than running on a treadmill for an hour. You never get bored because every class is different.
Man: Hmm, but I don't know how to box at all. Would I feel completely out of place?

Woman: Not at all! They have beginner classes three times a week where they teach you all the basics—how to stand properly, how to throw punches correctly, how to hold your hands up. The instructors are really patient, and everyone in the beginner classes is new too, so there's no pressure at all.
Man: What's a typical class like? How long does it last?

Woman: Classes are 45 minutes long. You start with a 10-minute warm-up—jumping jacks, stretching, that kind of thing. Then you do about 20 minutes of technique work on the bags, sometimes partner drills where you practice hitting pads. Then there's a 10-minute high-intensity circuit, and finally a 5-minute cool-down and stretch.
Man: That does sound like a good workout. How much does it cost? I'm on a pretty tight budget right now.

Woman: Their membership is 45 pounds a month, which includes unlimited classes. They also have a drop-in rate of 12 pounds per class if you want to try it out first without committing. Wait, actually, they're running a special this month—first class free for new people.
Man: That's a great deal! Do they provide the equipment, or do I need to buy my own gloves and wraps?

Woman: They have gloves you can borrow for free, and you can buy wraps there for 5 pounds if you don't have any. I'd recommend getting your own wraps eventually, but for the first class, you can just use theirs. Make sure to bring a water bottle and a towel though—you will sweat, guaranteed!
Man: What about the schedule? Do they have classes at reasonable times? I work 9 to 5, so I'd need to go in the evenings or on weekends.
Woman: Oh perfect, they have classes at 6:30 and 7:30 PM every weekday, and several classes throughout the day on Saturday. The Sunday schedule is lighter—just a morning class at 10.
Man: That actually works really well for me. Would you be free to go with me to a beginner class sometime this week? Having a friend there would make me feel less nervous about my first time.
Woman: Absolutely! I usually go on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. How about this Thursday at 6:30? We can grab a healthy dinner afterward at that new salad place nearby if you want.
Man: That sounds great! I'll take you up on that. Let me just make sure I bring comfortable clothes to work out in.
Woman: Perfect. Just wear something you can move in—trainers, shorts or sweatpants, a t-shirt. Oh, and don't eat a big meal right before class—you don't want to feel sluggish or get an upset stomach.
Man: Good advice! I really appreciate you telling me about this, Sarah. I've been meaning to start exercising more for ages, and this sounds much more fun than a regular gym.
Woman: I think you'll love it! Boxing is such a great stress reliever too after a long day at work. See you Thursday!

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Jennifer): Michael, have you started thinking about where you're going to live next year? The housing lottery for campus apartments opens next week, and I'm trying to decide if I want to apply again or find a place off campus.

Man (Michael): Oh, I'm glad you brought that up! I've actually been leaning toward moving off campus. I've lived in the dorms for two years now, and I'm ready for a change of pace. Plus, the campus apartments are almost as expensive as some places off campus, but you still have to share a room and follow all the dorm rules.

Woman: That's true, but isn't off-campus housing more of a hassle? You have to deal with landlords, pay utility bills, buy furniture... and then there's the commute if you don't live close enough to walk.

Man: Those are definitely things to consider, but I've been talking to some friends who live in that new apartment complex about a 15-minute walk from campus. The rent is actually cheaper than what we pay for campus housing, and you get your own bedroom. The utilities are included in the rent too, which is nice.
Woman: Really? That sounds pretty good. How much is it per person?

Man: For a four-bedroom apartment, it's about 650 dollars a month per person. That includes internet, water, electricity, everything. Compare that to the campus apartments, which are 800 dollars a month, and you still need a meal plan on top of that.
Woman: That is a big difference! But what about furniture? Do those apartments come furnished?

Man: The ones my friends live in don't come furnished, but most people just buy cheap furniture from secondhand stores or ask family members for hand-me-downs. I already have a desk and a chair from my grandparents, and I can get a bed pretty cheaply online. Some places do come furnished though—just a bit more expensive.
Woman: Hmm. I do like the idea of having my own kitchen. I'm getting really tired of eating campus food every night. It would be nice to cook my own meals and save money on the meal plan.

Man: That's one of the biggest advantages for me! My friends who live off campus say they save so much money by cooking instead of being on the meal plan. And you can eat whatever you want, whenever you want—no waiting in lines at the dining hall.
Woman: What about the lease? Do you have to sign for a full 12 months? That would be a problem because I'm going home for the summer, and I don't want to pay for an apartment I'm not using.

Man: A lot of places near campus do 12-month leases, but some offer 9-month leases specifically for students. Or if you sign a 12-month lease, you can usually sublet your room for the summer to someone taking summer classes. My friends did that last year and had no problem finding someone.

Woman: That's good to know. Would you want to get a place together with a few other people? It might be easier to find a bigger apartment if we're looking as a group. My roommate Rachel is also thinking about moving off campus.

Man: That's perfect! Let's do that. We can look for a three or four-bedroom place. I'll ask my friend who lives in that complex if he knows of any openings for next year. Also, there's a housing fair on campus this Wednesday where local landlords and property managers will have booths. We could go together and get some information.

Woman: That sounds like a plan! Let's meet at the student union at noon on Wednesday and go to the fair together. In the meantime, I'll talk to Rachel and see if she's definitely interested, and we can start figuring out what our budget is.
Man: Great. I'll start browsing some listings online too, just to get an idea of what's available. I'm actually pretty excited about this—having our own place will be such a nice change.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The history of handwriting is a fascinating journey that spans thousands of years, reflecting changes in technology, culture, and human communication. While handwriting might seem like a basic skill today, its development was crucial to the advancement of civilization.

The earliest form of writing, cuneiform, emerged in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE. It involved pressing wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets using a reed stylus. These early tablets were used primarily for record-keeping—tracking trade transactions, agricultural yields, and tax payments. Around the same time, hieroglyphic writing was developing in Egypt, though it served more ceremonial and religious purposes alongside administrative ones.

The invention of paper in China around 105 CE revolutionized writing, making it much more portable and accessible than clay tablets or papyrus. However, it wasn't until the spread of paper-making technology across the Middle East and into Europe by the 12th century that handwriting became more widespread beyond religious institutions and government offices.

The Middle Ages saw the development of various scripts in Europe, including Gothic script, which was characterized by dense, angular letters that allowed more text to fit on a page. Monks in monasteries were the primary scribes during this period, carefully copying religious texts and classical works by hand. The invention of the printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in the 15th century began to replace hand-copied books, but handwriting remained essential for correspondence, business records, and education.

The 19th century brought about the development of Spencerian script in the United States, an elegant, flowing style that became the standard taught in schools. This was later replaced by the Palmer Method in the early 20th century, which emphasized speed and efficiency over artistic flourishes, reflecting the faster pace of industrial society.

Today, in our digital age, many people worry that handwriting is becoming a lost art. Keyboards and touchscreens have replaced pens and pencils for most daily communication. However, educational researchers emphasize that handwriting remains important for cognitive development, particularly in children. Studies show that taking notes by hand improves retention and understanding compared to typing, and the physical act of writing helps with fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination. Many schools still teach cursive handwriting, though the amount of time dedicated to it has decreased significantly in recent decades.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Have you ever noticed that some people seem to adapt easily to new situations, while others struggle with even small changes in their routine? This difference can be partly explained by the concept of psychological resilience—the ability to bounce back from stress, adversity, and setbacks. While some people naturally seem more resilient than others, the good news is that resilience is not a fixed trait you're either born with or without. Research shows it's a set of skills that can be developed and strengthened over time.

So what exactly makes someone resilient? Psychologists have identified several key factors. One of the most important is having strong social support—people you can turn to for help, advice, or simply a listening ear when things go wrong. Studies consistently show that individuals with supportive relationships with family, friends, or community members handle stress much better than those who are socially isolated.

Another important factor is maintaining a positive but realistic outlook. Resilient people don't ignore problems or pretend everything is fine when it's not—instead, they tend to view difficulties as temporary challenges that can be overcome, rather than as permanent, insurmountable barriers. They also tend to have a strong sense of purpose or meaning in their lives, whether that comes from work, relationships, spirituality, or personal goals.

Practical problem-solving skills also contribute to resilience. People who are resilient don't just worry about problems—they actively look for solutions. They're able to break down overwhelming situations into small, manageable steps and take action rather than feeling helpless.

Self-care is another crucial but often overlooked aspect of resilience. Taking care of your physical health through regular exercise, adequate sleep, and proper nutrition gives you the energy and stamina to handle stress. Making time for activities you enjoy and setting boundaries to prevent burnout are also important.

If you feel you're not as resilient as you'd like to be, there are concrete steps you can take. Start by nurturing your relationships and reaching out to people when you need support. Work on reframing negative thoughts—when something bad happens, try to focus on what you can learn from the situation rather than dwelling on how terrible it is. Take care of your body, and make time for activities that help you recharge. And remember that setbacks are a normal part of life—everyone experiences them, and they don't define your worth or your future.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The electric scooter sharing phenomenon has taken cities around the world by storm over the past decade. These dockless scooters, which can be unlocked and rented through smartphone apps, promised to revolutionize urban transportation by providing a convenient, eco-friendly solution for the "last mile" problem—the distance between public transit stops and people's final destinations. But as the industry has matured, it has become clear that electric scooters come with both significant benefits and notable challenges.

On the positive side, electric scooters offer several clear advantages. They produce zero direct emissions, making them a much more environmentally friendly option than cars for short trips. They're also extremely convenient for quick trips—users can locate and unlock a scooter in seconds, ride it to their destination, and leave it wherever is convenient (within designated zones). For cities struggling with traffic congestion and limited parking, scooters can reduce the number of cars on the road. Studies in several major cities have found that a significant percentage of scooter trips would have otherwise been made by car or ride-hailing service, rather than replacing walking or public transit as critics initially feared.

However, the rapid, largely unregulated rollout of scooters led to numerous problems. One of the most visible issues was sidewalk clutter—companies flooded cities with thousands of scooters, often without permission, and users would leave them blocking sidewalks, building entrances, and wheelchair ramps. This created accessibility problems for pedestrians, particularly people with disabilities. Safety also became a major concern. Hospitals reported a surge in scooter-related injuries, including head injuries and broken bones, as many riders did not wear helmets and scooter brakes and maintenance were sometimes inadequate. There were also concerns about the lifespan of the scooters—early models often broke down within months, leading to questions about whether they were truly an environmentally sustainable option given the resources required to manufacture and replace them constantly.

In response to these issues, many cities have implemented regulations, including limits on the number of scooters allowed, requirements for dedicated parking zones, speed limits, and mandatory helmet laws. Scooter companies have also improved their designs, making scooters more durable and adding features like better brakes and lights. As cities and companies work together to address initial problems, electric scooters are evolving from a disruptive novelty into a more integrated part of urban transportation systems.
